findings.title: Remove unverified curl|sh remote installer from Dockerfile
findings.whyItBreaks: The new layer downloads a script over the network and pipes it straight into sh with no version pinning, checksum, or signature: whoever controls that URL gets arbitrary root code execution during image build, and its effects persist into every shipped image layer. The URL host is example.com — an IANA-reserved placeholder domain — and https://example.com/install.sh returns 404 (verified live), so the layer cannot perform any legitimate install; it is either a dangerous placeholder or a hijackable stub on the image's core build path.

findings.title: Fail build on curl HTTP errors instead of piping error page to sh
findings.whyItBreaks: The pipeline discards curl's failure signal three ways: no --fail (HTTP 4xx/5xx bodies are written to stdout as if they were the script — verified live that https://example.com/install.sh returns 404), -s suppresses curl's error output, and the pipe masks curl's exit status so only sh's status reaches the RUN layer. The 404 HTML body is what sh actually receives, so the build fails with an unrelated shell syntax error instead of curl's clear exit code 22 — and against a server that returns a parseable error body, failure would be indistinguishable from a real install.

findings.title: Remove unverified curl|sh remote code execution from build
findings.whyItBreaks: The added RUN executes whatever https://example.com/install.sh returns at build time with no version pinning, checksum, or signature. Image content becomes fully determined by a remote host (DNS/host takeover, compromised CDN, or a later URL swap all yield arbitrary code running as root inside the build). This is an unverified downloaded-and-executed artifact on a supply-chain surface.

findings.title: Dead URL plus missing --fail breaks build or silently skips install
findings.whyItBreaks: https://example.com/install.sh returns HTTP 404 (re-verified by live fetch). curl -sL without --fail exits 0 and pipes the 404 HTML body into sh, so RUN fails with a shell syntax error and the image cannot build at all. Conversely, on a connection failure curl outputs nothing and its nonzero exit status is discarded by the pipe, so sh reads empty input, exits 0, and the build succeeds while the intended tool is silently missing from the published image.

findings.title: Remove unpinned curl|sh remote script execution from image build
findings.whyItBreaks: The build now downloads https://example.com/install.sh and executes it with sh with zero integrity verification (CWE-494). Whatever the host serves at build time runs with full build privileges and can be baked into the shipped image; content can silently change between builds (non-reproducible, hijack/redirect -> arbitrary code in the artifact).

findings.title: Failed download silently succeeds: curl exit status lost across pipe
findings.whyItBreaks: The pipeline's exit status is sh's, not curl's: on transport failure curl -sL emits nothing (and -s hides the error), sh reads empty input and exits 0, so RUN succeeds and the image ships without the installed tool. Missing -f also means an HTTP error body (e.g. a 404 page) is piped into sh instead of failing the build.

findings.title: Restore completion guarantee: Run returns before goroutine sends finish
findings.whyItBreaks: Base Run (git show 5c8fe3c:src/worker.go) sent each result synchronously, so on return every send had completed and results arrived in job order — a caller could safely close(results) after Run returned. Head spawns one goroutine per job with no WaitGroup/done signal: Run returns immediately while goroutines remain blocked on results <- j*2. Any caller following the old contract and closing results after Run returns hits 'panic: send on closed channel'; results can also be lost if the process exits before the blocked goroutines run, and delivery order is now nondeterministic. This is a silent semantic change to an exported API with no compensating synchronization.

findings.title: Run returns before spawned goroutines send; no completion sync
findings.whyItBreaks: Base semantics: Run returned only after every `results <- j*2` send completed, so a caller could safely close(results) or proceed right after Run returned. Head spawns one bare goroutine per job with no WaitGroup/done channel, so Run returns immediately while sends are still pending. Any caller following the previously-correct pattern (close(results) after Run returns) now hits 'send on closed channel' panics; a caller that exits or advances a stage after return silently loses results. Output order also becomes nondeterministic. As an exported API, the function lost its completion guarantee with no replacement mechanism.

findings.title: Run returns before goroutines deliver results; leaks and send-on-closed panic
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run returned only after every job's result was sent (synchronous loop). The diff detaches each send into an unsynchronized goroutine and returns immediately. Consequences on the old contract: (1) a caller doing Run(ctx, jobs, ch); close(ch); for v := range ch now races in-flight sends against close -> 'send on closed channel' panic; (2) a caller reading len(jobs) values after Run returns observes zero or missing results; (3) a caller that never drains ch leaves every goroutine permanently blocked on send (one leaked goroutine per job). The function name/signature still promise 'run these jobs to completion', which the body no longer implements.

findings.title: Restore && in canDeleteRecord: || grants delete to every tenant member
findings.whyItBreaks: Base policy required isAdmin AND same-tenant (verified via git show 1d2409e). The new || means any authenticated non-admin session can delete ANY record whose tenantId matches its own (isAdmin check bypassed entirely), and any admin can delete records in ANY tenant. Deletion authority silently expands from 'admin within own tenant' to 'anyone within tenant or admin anywhere' — an authorization bypass on a destructive operation (record deletion = data loss). The function is exported (src/permissions.ts:12), so every consumer of this authorization contract gets the weakened policy immediately.

findings.title: AND→OR in canDeleteRecord enables cross-tenant and non-owner deletes
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous policy required BOTH isAdmin and tenant match. The new disjunction drops both constraints at once: (1) an admin session can now delete records belonging to ANY tenant (session.tenantId === record.tenantId is no longer enforced for admins), breaking tenant isolation; (2) any non-admin user can now delete ANY record in their own tenant regardless of ownership — RecordRef.ownerId (src/permissions.ts:9) is never consulted. Every current or future caller relying on this exported predicate to authorize record deletion will permit deletions the prior policy denied, i.e. silent data loss via authorized-looking deletes.

findings.title: Remove dbg!(items): it moves items, breaking compilation
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!` expands to `match $val { tmp => { eprintln!(..., &tmp); tmp } }`, taking its argument by value. `Vec<String>` is not Copy, so `dbg!(items);` at src/store.rs:2 moves `items`; the next statement `let total = items.len();` at src/store.rs:3 is then a use of a moved value and the crate fails to build with E0382 (`borrow of moved value: items`). Every downstream consumer of this crate is broken. Even if it compiled, dbg! would leak debug output to stderr in production paths.

findings.title: dbg!(items) moves items; subsequent items.len() fails to compile
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!` takes its argument by value: `dbg!(items);` expands to a block that moves `items` into the macro and drops it (return value discarded by the semicolon). The next statement `items.len()` at src/store.rs:3 then borrows a moved value, which is error E0382 (borrow of moved value: `items`). The crate does not compile at all — every consumer of this module is broken, and even if it compiled, `dbg!` would dump full item contents to stderr in production paths. Precondition substitution: field=items (moved @src/store.rs:2) → Consumer=borrow checker at `items.len()` @src/store.rs:3 → branch taken: reject (E0382) → effect: build failure, function unusable.

findings.title: dbg!(items) moves Vec, breaking compilation at items.len()
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!` expands to `match $val { tmp => { eprintln!(...); tmp } }`, taking ownership of its argument. `Vec<String>` is not Copy, so the statement `dbg!(items);` on line 2 moves `items` and drops the returned value; line 3's `items.len()` then borrows a moved value, producing error[E0382] borrow of moved value: `items`. The crate fails to compile, breaking every consumer of this public function (no in-repo callers exist, but `process` is `pub`). Even if ownership were not an issue, `dbg!` dumps argument values to stderr on every call — leftover debug output in a library path.

findings.title: Async gap in reserve() breaks atomic check-then-act, allowing oversell
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously reserve() was synchronous and therefore atomic under the JS event loop: read remaining, guard, write remaining-1 could not interleave. The diff adds `await this.store.save(...)` (src/inventory.ts:17) between the guard (line 16) and the write (line 18). Substitution with stock=1: call A reads remaining=1, awaits save and suspends; call B then reads remaining=1 (A has not written yet), also passes the guard and awaits save; both resume, both set stock to 0 and both resolve true. Two reservations are granted for one unit; with stock=N, two interleaved calls both read N and both persist N-1, collapsing two decrements into one persisted write (lost update, oversold inventory). Concurrency is the expected mode for this API — it was made async precisely because persistence is async I/O, and Inventory.reserve is an exported public path.

findings.title: Async gap between stock check and decrement enables oversell
findings.whyItBreaks: Base reserve() was synchronous, so read-check-write on this.stock was atomic under JS's single thread. The diff adds `await this.store.save(...)` (src/inventory.ts:17) between the guard `remaining <= 0` (line 16) and the write `this.stock.set` (line 18). Two concurrent calls for the same SKU with remaining=1 both read 1, both pass the guard while the first is suspended at the await, both call store.save(sku, 0), and both return true: two reservations granted against one unit (oversell) and the persisted value written twice from stale state.

findings.title: Migrate all reserve() callers for the sync-to-async signature switch
findings.whyItBreaks: Public exported method changed from `boolean` to `Promise<boolean>`. Any pre-existing caller written against the base API that branches on the result (`if (inventory.reserve(sku)) ...`) now evaluates a Promise object, which is always truthy — out-of-stock requests take the success path with no error raised (TS does not flag Promise-in-condition without extra lint). The new required constructor arg (line 8) additionally makes `new Inventory()` from old call sites crash on first reserve ('Cannot read properties of undefined'). Failure mode is silent, so this must be resolved before merge, not after.

findings.title: Serialize check-then-write in reserve(); await adds lost-update race
findings.whyItBreaks: Base version was fully synchronous (verified via `git show 7c79ad8:src/inventory.ts`), so read→guard→write was atomic per event-loop turn. The inserted `await this.store.save(...)` (line 17) yields between the guard (line 16) and the decrement (line 18). Two concurrent `reserve('x')` calls with remaining=1 both read 1, both pass the guard, both save 0, and both return true — one unit double-reserved. With remaining=N, overlapping calls both compute N-1 and the second save overwrites the first, losing a decrement, so the store overcounts and a later oversell becomes possible.

findings.title: backoff() now returns ms but retry.ts still multiplies by 1000 (1000x sleep)
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff changes backoff()'s unit from seconds (min(30, 2**attempt)) to milliseconds (min(30_000, 2**attempt * 1000)) and updates src/net/poll.ts:4 accordingly. The other caller, src/jobs/retry.ts:12 (`await sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`), was not updated and still treats the return value as seconds. Substitution: attempt a=0 → old path slept 1*1000=1s; new path sleeps 1000*1000=1,000,000ms (~16.7min). a=5 → old 30s; new 30_000*1000=30,000,000ms (~8.3h). Every failed attempt in retry<T>() now stalls minutes-to-hours before retrying, breaking the retry workflow.

findings.title: backoff() now returns ms but retry.ts still multiplies by 1000 (1000x sleep)
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff re-units backoff() from seconds to milliseconds (min(30000, 2**attempt*1000)) and updates src/net/poll.ts:4 to match, but misses the second caller src/jobs/retry.ts:12 which still executes `await sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`. Substitution: a=0 → old sleep = min(30,1)*1000 = 1,000ms; new sleep = min(30000,1000)*1000 = 1,000,000ms (~16.7 min). a=1 → 2,000,000ms; a≥5 (cap) → 30,000*1000 = 30,000,000ms (~8.3h). Every failed fn() call now stalls the retry loop for minutes-to-hours instead of seconds, hanging any workflow using retry().

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside transaction break transfer atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: In base (verified via `git show 15ae7bc:app/transfer.py`) the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs ran inside one `with db.transaction():` block — all-or-nothing. The refactor keeps only `_record_ledger` inside the block (app/transfer.py:23) and calls `_apply_balances` at app/transfer.py:24 AFTER the transaction commits. If the debit UPDATE succeeds but the credit UPDATE raises (DB error, lock timeout, crash between statements), the debit is already committed with no matching credit and no ledger rollback path: money is removed from `from_acct` and never arrives at `to_acct`, while the ledger row claims a completed transfer. Even absent a crash, the debit and credit are no longer atomic with each other or with the ledger record, so any single-statement failure leaves persisted inconsistent state where base guaranteed none.

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside transaction break transfer atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: At base (fdae678) all three statements — ledger INSERT, debit UPDATE, credit UPDATE — ran inside one `with db.transaction():` block, so they committed or rolled back together. At head, only `_record_ledger` runs inside the transaction (app/transfer.py:23); `_apply_balances` executes at app/transfer.py:24 AFTER the transaction context exits and commits. If the process crashes or any error occurs between commit and the balance updates (or between the two UPDATEs at app/transfer.py:9-16, which now run with no transaction around them), the ledger row is already durably committed while balances are unapplied or half-applied: money is debited from `from_acct` without crediting `to_acct`, or the books record a transfer that never touched balances. This is a silent, permanent financial-state corruption on a core money path.
